ta-l1d9q2-d1e97.summary: Transitional paragraph opening the inquiry into the Son's coeternity with the Father in two articles: whether the Father is in any way prior to the Son, and, if not and the generation is eternal, by what verbs it should be signified.

ta-l1d9q2-d1e109.summary: First argument that the Father is prior to the Son. Generation relates to beginning as corruption relates to ceasing, and whatever is corrupted ceases to be. So whatever is generated begins to be through generation, and the Son began to be and is posterior to the Father.
claims: Whatever is generated begins to be.

ta-l1d9q2-d1e112.summary: Second argument. Nothing receives except what it does not have, and whatever is generated receives being from the generator, so before generation it did not have being.
claims: One receives only what one lacks.

ta-l1d9q2-d1e115.summary: Third argument. A principle is naturally prior to that of which it is the principle, and the Father is the principle of the Son, so he is prior at least by nature, if not in time.
claims: A principle is naturally prior to what it originates.

ta-l1d9q2-d1e119.summary: Fourth argument. Giving being is a dignity, and the Father gives his being to the Son, so the Father is prior at least in dignity.
claims: Giving being is a dignity.

ta-l1d9q2-d1e122.summary: Sed contra. Whatever something is prior to is not simply first. If the Father were prior to the Son, the Son would not be simply first. But all say that God is the first principle (the Philosopher), so the Son would not be God, which is what the Arians grant.
claims: What has something prior to it is not simply first.
Priority of the Father would deny the Son's divinity, as the Arians held.

ta-l1d9q2-d1e125.summary: Thomas's determination. The Father is in no way prior to the Son, not in duration, nature, understanding, or dignity. In Father and Son only two things can be considered. What is absolute is common to both and gives neither priority, since the divine essence is indivisible. What is relative gives none either, since relatives are simultaneous by nature (the Philosopher), in time (posited together and destroyed together), and in understanding (each defined by the other). Among humans the one who is father, like Socrates, is prior to the one who is son, like Plato, but father and son as relatives are simultaneous in all these ways. So the Father is in no way prior to the Son, either by what is absolute or by what is relative.
claims: The Father is not prior to the Son in duration, nature, understanding, or dignity.
Relatives as such are simultaneous by nature, in time, and in understanding.
In God both the absolute (the essence) and the relative (the persons) exclude priority.

ta-l1d9q2-d1e128.summary: Reply to the first argument. The generation opposed to corruption is a change, and beginning is always attached to such generation. Generation in God is not a change but an operation of the divine nature as it is in the Father. A natural operation always accompanies what it belongs to, so since the divine nature in the Father is eternal, the generation is eternal.
claims: Divine generation is not a change but an eternal operation of the divine nature.

ta-l1d9q2-d1e131.summary: Reply to the second argument. What receives something does not have it from itself, but it does not follow that it does not have it simply, since the receiving may never have begun. So the Son received being from the Father and does not have being from himself, but received it from the Father from eternity.
claims: Receiving from another is compatible with eternal possession.

ta-l1d9q2-d1e134.summary: Reply to the third argument. A principle can be considered as the thing that is the principle, which is naturally prior to what it originates, or by the relation of principle, by which it is naturally simultaneous with what it originates. If something had both its being something and its being related from the same source, it would be wholly simultaneous by nature with its correlative. In God the Father has from the same source that he is someone and that he is Father, so he is simultaneous by nature with the Son, not only as Father but simply.
claims: The Father is constituted as someone by the same paternity by which he is Father, so he is simply simultaneous with the Son.
concepts: principle as thing vs. as relation

ta-l1d9q2-d1e138.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. The property by which the Father gives being is his dignity. But dignity belongs to what is absolute, so the same dignity is in Father and Son: what is paternity in the Father is filiation in the Son, just as paternity in the Father is the divine essence or goodness, and the numerically same essence or goodness is filiation in the Son.
claims: Father and Son share one dignity, which is paternity in one and filiation in the other.

ta-l1d9q2-d1e150.summary: First argument that divine generation should be signified in the present tense. The present best fits eternity, since it has no succession, and divine generation is eternal.
claims: The present tense best fits eternity.

ta-l1d9q2-d1e153.summary: Second argument from Avicenna's distinction between an agent that is cause only of becoming, which influences its effect only while it is coming to be, and an agent that is principle of being, which never ceases to influence its effect while it exists. The Father is principle of the Son's being, not of his becoming, since the Son is not made, so as long as the Son exists the Father gives him being, and this giving is generation. Since the Son is most truly said always to be rather than to have been, it would be truer to say he is always being born (semper nasci) than always born (semper natus).
claims: A cause of being acts continuously as long as its effect exists.
The Father is principle of the Son's being, not of his becoming.

ta-l1d9q2-d1e156.summary: Sed contra. What is always in becoming is imperfect, and 'always being born' signifies something as always in becoming, so it signifies imperfection and is not properly said of the Son, from whom all imperfection is excluded.
claims: What is always in becoming is imperfect.

ta-l1d9q2-d1e160.summary: Second sed contra. Whatever follows generation in our mode of understanding is like its terminus, and the relation of filiation follows generation so understood. The terminus of generation is signified by the past, not the present, so the Son is more truly called born (natus) than being born (nascens).
claims: The terminus of generation is signified by the past tense.

ta-l1d9q2-d1e163.summary: Thomas's determination. As shown in Distinction 8, no tensed verb perfectly represents eternity. So the eternal generation of the Son is not sufficiently expressed by a verb of any one tense and can be signified by verbs of different tenses, attributing to it whatever is perfect in each and excluding all imperfection. In lower generation and every becoming, being is imperfect, since such things exist only in becoming. Perfection comes only when the becoming ends, and then the creature's generation no longer exists, as at the terminus of motion there is no motion. In divine generation perfection and being are found together. To signify the being of divine generation, which never passes, we can use the present ('the Son is begotten by the Father'). To signify its perfection we can use the past ('the Son is born'). To include both, it is most fitting to say 'always born' (semper natus): 'always' signifies the unfailing being of the generation and the past tense its perfection. 'Always being born' would signify only the unfailing being, not the perfection, so 'always born' is better. For other divine things not signified as in becoming, the present tense is more fitting.
claims: No single tense perfectly signifies the eternal generation.
In divine generation perfection and being coincide, unlike in creaturely becoming.
'Semper natus' best signifies the generation, joining unfailing being (semper) with perfection (natus).

ta-l1d9q2-d1e166.summary: Reply to the first argument. Although the present best fits eternity, since it posits being in act, for things signified by way of becoming it implies imperfection, since such things are imperfect while they exist. For them the past is more fitting, especially with something added to signify unfailingness.
claims: For things signified as becoming, the present implies imperfection; the past with 'always' is preferable.

ta-l1d9q2-d1e169.summary: Reply to the second argument. Avicenna's reasoning proves that the being of divine generation never passes, which the present signifies. But because generation is signified by way of becoming, that mode of signifying implies some imperfection, so the past must be used, as the sed contra arguments conclude.
claims: The continuous causation of the Son's being is real, but the past tense is needed to exclude the imperfection of becoming.

ta-l1d9q2-d1e178.summary: An expositio textus on Distinction 9. (1) Augustine argues from 'Christ the power and wisdom of God' (1 Cor. 1:24) that the Father never lacked the Son. The objection is that if this means essential wisdom, the Father would have it even without the Son, and if begotten wisdom, the Father is not wise by it. Thomas answers that it means essential wisdom as appropriated to the Son, in which the notion of what is proper is understood, or better begotten wisdom, which the Father has though he is not wise by it; it would be absurd for God to have a wisdom he did not always have. (2) To the objections that there is no motion in relation, and that God becomes Creator without change, so he could become Father without change: new relations cannot arise really in something without motion, since relation follows motion as equality follows growth; and God's relation to creatures is real only in the creature, while paternity is really in God as constitutive of a person, so God could not newly become Father without changing. (3) The 'voice of angels' is their speech in assumed bodies or their spiritual ordering of concepts for communication. (4) The temporal generation is ineffable as terminating in personal union with God, though in some way effable on the side of the body taken from the Virgin. (5) The likeness of light and splendour is to be applied to eternal generation by continuity, not by the interruption that marks the sun's rising. (6) Hilary's argument that the living God's power produces something living is set out as two syllogisms, and the Son lives with the numerically same life of the Father, since he is not begotten by division or change; the Son images the Father in everything except innascibility. (7) 'Infinite' begetting and being born is meant negatively, as unbounded, not quantitatively, which would make the generation imperfect.
claims: Christ is the begotten wisdom the Father has, though the Father is not wise by it.
New real relations require change, so God could not newly become Father without change, though he becomes Creator without change.
The Son lives with the Father's numerically identical life and images him in all but innascibility.
The generation is 'infinite' negatively, not quantitatively.

ta-l1d9q2-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Question 2 introduces the Son's coeternity with the Father in two articles: whether the Father is in any way prior, and how the eternal generation should be expressed in tensed verbs.

ta-l1d9q2-Dd1e101.summary: Article 1 asks whether the Father is in any way prior to the Son. Thomas holds that he is not, in duration, nature, understanding, or dignity. What is absolute in them is the one indivisible essence, and what is relative is simultaneous by nature, time, and understanding. Divine generation is an eternal operation, not a change, and the Son receives being eternally. The Father is constituted as someone by the same paternity by which he is Father, so he is simply simultaneous with the Son, and the one dignity is paternity in the Father and filiation in the Son.
claims: The Father is in no way prior to the Son.
Relatives as such are simultaneous; in God the Father is constituted by paternity and so is simultaneous with the Son simply.

ta-l1d9q2-Dd1e142.summary: Article 2 asks how the eternal generation should be signified. Since no tense perfectly signifies eternity, each tense is used for what is perfect in it. In divine generation being and perfection coincide, unlike in creaturely becoming. The present can signify its unfailing being, the past its perfection, and 'always born' (semper natus) signifies both best, better than 'always being born', which omits perfection. Avicenna's continuous causation of being shows the generation never passes, but the mode of signifying becoming calls for the past tense.
claims: 'Semper natus' is the most fitting expression of the eternal generation.

ta-l1d9q2-Dd1e173.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 9 glosses Augustine's argument from Christ as God's wisdom. It explains why God could not newly become Father without change though he becomes Creator without change, and treats angelic speech, the effability of the temporal generation, the light–splendour analogy, Hilary's argument that the Son lives with the Father's identical life, and the negative sense of 'infinite' generation.
claims: God could not become Father without change, since paternity is a real relation in God, unlike his relation to creatures.
The Son shares the Father's numerically identical life.

ta-l1d9q2.summary: Quaestio 2 of Book I, Distinction 9 treats the Son's coeternity with the Father. Article 1 denies any priority of the Father, whether in duration, nature, understanding, or dignity. The essence is one and indivisible, and relatives as such are simultaneous, and the Father is constituted by the very paternity by which he is related to the Son. Article 2 holds that the eternal generation, in which being and perfection coincide, is best expressed by 'always born' (semper natus), uniting unfailing being with completed perfection. The Expositio explains, against Arius, that God could not newly become Father without change, since paternity is a real constitutive relation in God, unlike his relation to creatures. It also glosses patristic arguments for the Son's eternal and living generation.
claims: The Father is in no way prior to the Son; Father and Son are coeternal.
The eternal generation is best signified by 'semper natus'.
Paternity, unlike God's relation to creatures, is a real relation in God, so it cannot be newly acquired without change.
